title: Commitment lattice and reserve-fallback guidelines for Dedicated capacity
creator: Ava Morgan
description:
Background: Customers increasingly ask for flexible reserved GPU commitments that balance predictability and cost. Current reserve products are either long-term static commitments or short-term burst credits; neither handles steady-but-bursty workloads with variable latency requirements and enterprise SLA profiles. This ticket defines a commitment lattice (multi-tier reserve SKUs + soft credits) and a reserve-fallback playbook to cover preemption, graceful degradation, and contractual language for enterprise SQs.

Objectives:
1) Define a compact SKU lattice that maps to common customer profiles (steady baseline, elastic peak, strict-p99 latency tier).
2) Design a reserve-fallback policy so customers have predictable fallthrough behaviors when reserved pool is saturated (soft credits, minute-level top-ups, cross-region fallbacks).
3) Specify pricing experiments and billing examples to measure unit economics vs. current offerings.
4) Produce contract and security-questionnaire guidance that addresses encryption, BYOK/KMS, network isolation, and audit log retention for each SKU tier.

Why this matters: Offers customers predictable cost with better utilization while protecting Redwood from unbounded burst exposure. Helps close larger enterprise deals by codifying SLA glidepaths and fallback guarantees in contracts and the SQ response templates.
acceptance_criteria: SKU lattice documented with three primary tiers and optional add-ons (burst credits, regional isolation)
Pricing experiment matrix and billing scenarios (5 customer archetypes) captured in PRD
Reserve-fallback policy defined (order of fallbacks, time-to-preempt, grace windows, notification triggers)
Legal/finance draft contract clauses for fallback and overage handling ready for review
Security questionnaire answers and template sections prepared for tiered SKUs and handed to Security for approval

notes_and_tradeoffs:
Trade-offs considered: 1) Simpler two-tier model (Reserved vs. On-demand) reduces sales complexity but yields poor match for mixed workloads. 2) Aggressive soft-credit refill increases customer experience but risks higher infra costs — mitigated via time-windowed caps and priority-based throttling. 3) Cross-region fallback reduces tail latency guarantees; instead prefer explicit opt-in region-fallback add-on for Enterprise tier.

Measurement plan: Run A/B pricing experiment with 10 pilot customers across 3 archetypes for 60 days. Track metrics: effective cost per GPU-hour, p99 latency breach count, fallback activation rate, churn intent signals, net-new ARR uplift. Success criteria: >10% improvement in gross margin vs current burstless reserved offering and customer NPS >= 8 in pilot group.
implementation_steps: 1) Finalize SKU lattice and pricing bands. 2) Legal: prepare contract addendum and fallback clause. 3) Engineering: estimate infra change to support minute-top-ups, per-customer credit buckets, and policy enforcement. 4) Billing: add meter + invoice preview for top-ups and soft-credit consumption. 5) Security: draft SQ answers for new SKU features (BYOK, audit logs, region isolation). 6) Launch pilot with 10 customers; monitor metrics and iterate.
billing_examples: Example A (Startup): Baseline SKU (4 reserved GPUs) + 100 burst-min credits monthly = $X/month (vs On-demand $Y). Example B (Retail): Performance SKU (16 reserved GPUs, performance SLA) + auto-top-up capped at 120 minutes/day = $Z/month. Include tokenized sample invoice mock in PRD.
open_questions: 1) What is the acceptable top-up pricing delta vs on-demand during pilot? 2) Should we allow unlimited soft credits for Enterprise with revenue-share guardrails? 3) What telemetry surface is required to show customers fallbacks in Console?
decision_log: 2026-03-12: Decided to proceed with three-tier lattice and capped soft-credit top-ups for pilot. Cross-region fallback will be an opt-in add-on. Legal to draft fallback clause limiting automatic top-ups to pre-approved budgets.
security_summary: Security impact: Enterprise SKU requires BYOK (KMS integration), tenant isolation checks, region-specific audit retention. Proposed SQ answers include references to existing KMS integrations, VPC peering controls, and a new log-retention option. Security review requested and flagged in comments.
